title_en: Quit Your Job, Live Off an ETF?
title_zh: 辞掉工作、靠 ETF 过活？——对话 Bloomberg Money 记者 Zitia Song 与 Green Ocean Global Advisors 理财顾问 Mark Moberg
subtitle_zh: 聊衍生品收益型 ETF 如何支撑「分红游牧族」提前退休，以及背后的收益、税务与风险权衡。
summary_zh: 本期 Trillions 由 Joel Weber 与 Eric Balchunas 主持，围绕 Bloomberg Money 一篇《分红游牧族（dividend nomads）》报道展开，请来该文作者、个人投资记者 Zitia Song 与报道消息源、Green Ocean Global Advisors 理财顾问 Mark Moberg（人在葡萄牙）。核心议题是衍生品收益型 ETF（derivative income ETFs）如何支撑一部分人'提前退休、环游世界'。Balchunas 把这类产品称为'制造出来的收益'（manufactured yield），形态包括备兑看涨期权 ETF（covered call ETFs）与自动赎回型产品（auto-callables）——后者规模从去年底的 5.8 亿美元飙升至逾 50 亿美元，整个类别过去三年资产翻了两番、如今约 2700 亿美元。Song 讲述她在 Reddit 挖到的用户，如一位 40 岁美国人在韩国靠分红覆盖全部开销；也点出风险承受能力差异极大，以及高收入证明虽有助于拿签证、却可能牺牲长远利益的两难。Moberg 强调客户多为旅居海外的创业者，主张让人'睁大眼睛'了解风险后再决定，并称永远不要低估'韧劲'（grit）。节目还延伸到 FIRE 运动、AI 取代工作的焦虑如何助推这股潮流，以及这类 ETF 是否本身在压制波动率——引出 JP Morgan 的 Bram Kaplan 观点与 Balchunas 所谓'Vanguard 看跌期权'（the Vanguard put）的讨论。
description: Quit Your Job, Live Off an ETF?

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客。电台。

turns.en: News.
turns.zh: 新闻。

turns.en: Welcome to Trillions. I'm Joel Weber.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Trillions。我是 Joel Weber。

turns.en: And I'm Eric Balchunas.
turns.zh: 我是 Eric Balchunas。

turns.en: Eric, there's a headline recently from our colleagues at Bloomberg Money. The headline, the dividend nomads investing their way out of the nine to five. And we immediately started to email it to each other because.
turns.zh: Eric，最近咱们 Bloomberg Money 的同事出了个报道，标题是「分红游牧族（dividend nomads）：靠投资摆脱朝九晚五」。我俩立马就把它转来转去、互相发邮件，因为——

turns.en: There are ETFs.
turns.zh: 因为里头用到了 ETF。

turns.en: In the story that we've talked sometimes about on Trillions, but boy, this really gave me some yearnings to change my life. And these ETFs, I felt like were worth coming back to and talking about again.
turns.zh: 这篇报道里用到的 ETF，我们在 Trillions 上有时也聊过。但说真的，这篇看得我心里直痒痒，都想改变一下自己的生活了。我觉得这些 ETF 值得再拿出来好好聊一聊。

turns.en: These are derivative income ETFs. What is that category?
turns.zh: 这些都是衍生品收益型 ETF（derivative income ETFs）。这个类别到底是怎么回事？

turns.en: Yeah, we used to call it manufactured yield. It's basically a way to increase the income or yield that you get. People love income. It's popular across the world. It's one consistent across the world. In the US in particular, cover call ETFs are one form auto callables. And the cover call can range from like, it depends on where you write the call option. But if it's close to the money, they can yield a lot. Now, some of this is just taking your total return and giving it to yourself in income. But there are huge hits. We had that one guy on a couple of years back who liked the yield max funds and he was using the income to get a mortgage. So there's many reasons that this can be helpful for people. And ETFs, again, they're just very convenient. And I think the reason I like this article is that a lot of times the articles don't actually talk to the real people using them. The face is behind the flows. This one had like multiple people out there who were using the income to do some interesting things, including travel the world. So this is really great to get through the sort of business part of this into the actual retail investor to find out what they're up to.
turns.zh: 对，我们过去管它叫「制造出来的收益」（manufactured yield）。说白了，就是一种提高你到手收入或收益率的办法。大家都喜欢现金流收入，这类产品在全世界都很受欢迎，而且各地的形态也相当一致。尤其在美国，备兑看涨期权 ETF（covered call ETFs）是其中一种形式，还有自动赎回型产品（auto callables）。备兑期权的收益率高低，得看你在哪个行权价卖出看涨期权（write the call option）；如果卖得接近现价（close to the money），收益率可以很高。当然，这里面有一部分其实只是把你的总回报（total return）拆出来、以收入的形式发给你自己。但它确实有实实在在的用处。几年前我们请过一位嘉宾，他很喜欢 YieldMax 那类基金，还靠这些收入去申请房贷。所以这类产品能帮到人的理由有很多。而且 ETF 用起来非常方便。我喜欢这篇文章的地方在于：很多报道其实并不会去采访真正在用这些产品的人，也就是「资金流背后的那些面孔」（the faces behind the flows）。而这篇里出现了好几位，他们拿这些收入去做一些很有意思的事，包括环游世界。所以能跳出纯业务层面、真正走进散户投资者、看看他们到底在做什么，实在是太好了。

turns.en: Joining us on this episode, Zitia Song, who's a personal investing reporter with Bloomberg Money. She's the one who wrote the story. As well as Mark Moberg, who's a financial advisor with Green Ocean Global Advisors. He's a source in the story, based in Portugal. I think I have more notes to take. This time on Trillions, derivative income ETFs. Zitia, Mark, thanks for joining us on Trillions.
turns.zh: 本期做客节目的两位嘉宾：一位是 Bloomberg Money 的个人投资记者 Zitia Song，这篇报道就是她写的；另一位是 Green Ocean Global Advisors 的理财顾问 Mark Moberg，他是报道里的一个消息源，人在葡萄牙。我这次得多记点笔记了。这一期 Trillions 的主题是衍生品收益型 ETF。Zitia、Mark，感谢二位做客 Trillions。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Glad to be here.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里。

turns.en: Zitra, I want to start with you.
turns.zh: Zitia，我想先从你开始。

turns.en: I just got such FOMO from reading this story, mainly because the people that you managed to find are living a better version of a life than I am.
turns.zh: 我读这篇报道的时候，真是各种羡慕嫉妒（FOMO），主要因为你找到的这些人，过的日子比我这版本好太多了。

turns.en: Who's doing this and how did you find them? Yeah.
turns.zh: 都有谁在这么过？你又是怎么找到他们的？

turns.en: Honestly, when I first reached out to them, I also had that yearning. I was like, I want to live that life. So I started off looking into auto callable ETFs, which you guys have talked about before on the podcast. And it's a very complex product. So I was trying to figure out, like, who's really using these? Because these are really the new hot thing in the ETF world. And just to put into context, I think at the end of last year, the total asset in this industry or in this space for Auto Colorballs is just $ 580 million. And now it's over $ 5 billion. So I started like digging on Reddit and see who's talking about these tickers. And one guy actually emailed me. Sadly, I couldn't include him in the story, but he was detailing how he's using auto-callable ETFs and like the covered call ETFs, all these derivative income products to live in South Korea. He's an American 40-year-old. And he gave me a detailed daily routine. He serves a lot. He teaches English at local universities. But most of his or actually all of his monthly budget were sponsored by these dividends from the high yield products. And he told me this. He's like, you know what? I don't really need to understand how these products work. I just need to know that they can give me income. And it's the fund manager's job to know how these work. Yeah.
turns.zh: 说实话，我最初联系他们的时候，自己心里也有那种向往，想着「我也想过那样的生活」。所以我一开始去研究自动赎回型 ETF（auto-callable ETFs），你们之前在播客里也聊过。这是一种非常复杂的产品，我就想搞清楚到底是谁在真金白银地用它们，因为这确实是 ETF 圈里最新的大热门。给大家一个概念：我记得去年底，这个自动赎回型（auto-callables）领域的总规模才 5.8 亿美元，现在已经超过 50 亿美元了。于是我就泡在 Reddit 上挖，看谁在讨论这些代码（tickers）。还真有一个人给我发了邮件。可惜最后没能把他写进报道里，但他详细讲了自己怎么靠自动赎回型 ETF、备兑期权 ETF 这些衍生品收益产品，在韩国过日子的。他是个 40 岁的美国人。他给了我一份很详细的日常作息。他做很多事——在当地大学教英语，但他每月开销的绝大部分，或者说全部，都是靠这些高收益产品派发的分红来覆盖的。他还跟我说：「你知道吗？我其实不太需要搞懂这些产品是怎么运作的，我只需要知道它们能给我带来收入就行。搞懂它们怎么运作，是基金经理的事。」

turns.en: Many things go wrong with similar words, but it looks like he's kind of living a life that is not a nine to five office job.
turns.zh: 这里面很多事情都可能出岔子，但看起来他确实过上了一种不用朝九晚五坐办公室的生活。

turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: For the most part. Seems like he's doing whatever he wants. Why do you, from everybody that you spoke to, why is this happening now? What's changed?
turns.zh: 大体上是这样。看起来他想干什么就干什么。那从你聊过的所有人来看，为什么这股潮流是现在冒出来的？发生了什么变化？

turns.en: So COVID really popularized this idea of remote work. So people are more familiar with kind of a work culture transformation where they can work from anywhere. and do whatever job that they can come up with. Also, at the meantime, governments have come up with a bunch of visa programs that made it much easier for foreigners to live in their country and work in their country. Of course, those visa programs have kind of dwindled a little bit in recent years. And finally, there's an emergence of a bunch of these derivative income products. Actually, over the past three years, the assets within these products have quadrupled to now a 270 billion industry. Wow.
turns.zh: 新冠疫情真正把「远程办公」这个概念普及开了。所以大家对这种工作文化的转变更习惯了——可以在任何地方工作，干任何自己想得出来的活儿。与此同时，各国政府也推出了一堆签证项目，让外国人来本国生活、工作变得容易多了。当然，这几年这类签证项目有点缩水。最后，就是这一大批衍生品收益产品的出现。实际上过去三年里，这类产品的资产规模翻了两番，如今已经是一个 2700 亿美元的行业了。哇。

turns.en: What do you think you learned from talking to these folks?
turns.zh: 你觉得跟这些人聊下来，学到了什么？

turns.en: I learned that people have very different risk tolerance. So, I mean, we all dream of quitting our 9 to 5 and go live somewhere fun and be able to dictate what you do every day. And these people are are doing it to different degrees. So like they put different portion of their of their total nest egg into these products. And it really is up to individuals for risk tolerance, what they are able to tolerate, what they are willing to compromise. And I've learned that they also are treating this as an experiment themselves. Like no one's sure of whether this will work out or not, or even in the long term, like when they have the baby or when they reach retirement of like 60 or something, whether this will work. But everyone's treating this as an experiment to see, okay, this worked or this not.
turns.zh: 我发现大家的风险承受能力差别非常大。我是说，我们都梦想着辞掉朝九晚五的工作，去一个好玩的地方生活，能自己说了算每天干什么。而这些人正在不同程度地把这个梦想变成现实。他们把各自「老本」（nest egg）里不同比例的钱投进这些产品。这真的取决于个人的风险承受能力——你能承受多少、你愿意在哪些地方妥协。我还发现，他们自己也把这当成一场实验。没人敢肯定这么做到底行不行得通，甚至从长远看——比如等他们有了孩子、或者到了六十岁退休的时候——这套还灵不灵，也没人说得准。但每个人都在拿它做实验，看看「行，这个成立，或者这个不成立」。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Speaking of experiments, Mark, you're in Portugal.
turns.zh: 说到实验，Mark，你人在葡萄牙。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And I'm curious, how did you end up there? And are you using derivative income ETFs to support your lifestyle in Portugal?
turns.zh: 我很好奇，你当初是怎么去到那儿的？还有，你在葡萄牙的生活，是靠衍生品收益型 ETF 来支撑的吗？

turns.en: The second question, no, I'm not. But we got here actually through my wife's work. Her company had a expat assignment and we thought, why not? Let's try it out. And Portugal sounds like, you know, was a pretty good place to go if I was going to have to choose a place. So, you know, we decided to pack up about five years ago.
turns.zh: 第二个问题，答案是否定的，我没有靠它。不过我们之所以来这儿，其实是因为我太太的工作。她公司有一个外派（expat）机会，我们就想「干嘛不试试呢」。而且葡萄牙听起来是个挺不错的地方——真要选一个地方去的话。所以大概五年前，我们决定收拾行囊搬了过来。

turns.en: So how do you feel about this category of ETFs as a financial advisor?
turns.zh: 那么作为一名理财顾问，你怎么看这一类 ETF？

turns.en: I think it might be a good tool, but it might be for the wrong job for many people. I would say that, you know, let's talk about a fish. You take a fish, swims good, but you're not going to take it out of the water and ask it to walk. And that's what my concern is, is that you're trying to get equity yields out of an investment that you're treating, in many people's minds, you're treating it as fixed income. So that's really my concern. And there's also some other things, the way they're taxed in Portugal. I can only speak to that, to my country. It's taxed differently than it would be in the United States. So there's that issue as well.
turns.zh: 我觉得它可能是个不错的工具，但对很多人来说，也许是用错了地方。打个比方，说说一条鱼吧：鱼在水里游得很好，可你不会把它捞出水、叫它走路。我的担心就在于此——你想从一笔投资里榨出股票级的收益（equity yields），但在很多人心里，他们其实是把它当成固定收益（fixed income）产品来对待的。所以这才是我真正担心的地方。另外还有一些别的问题，比如它们在葡萄牙的征税方式——这个我只能就我自己的国家来说——它跟在美国的征税方式是不一样的。所以还有那方面的问题。

turns.en: So how often do you have clients coming to you, asking you about these? Because as Zetia's story makes clear, there is a... fantasy that these products seem to evoke because it looks like, hey, this thing, I put some money aside, something happens, and then I get an income stream.
turns.zh: 那经常会有客户来找你、问起这些产品吗？因为正如 Zitia 的报道所揭示的，这些产品似乎勾起了一种……幻想，看上去就是：嘿，这个东西，我放一笔钱进去，中间发生了点什么，然后我就得到了一串现金流收入。

turns.en: That sounds pretty great. How often are you hearing from people?
turns.zh: 这听起来相当美好。那你多久会听到有人来问一次？

turns.en: Interestingly, I hear more from people who are at the margins. They're trying to stretch every cent out of their savings to try to make this move. So it And part of that is because to qualify for a D7 visa here in Portugal, you have to show a certain amount of income. Well, with a high income like showing from a product like these, it makes it easier to achieve to hit that bar. The problem is, as we're talking about, is that you're solving one problem and maybe creating another by having a product that's not really in your long-term interest. It gets complicated. It gets you over here, but then what do you do once you're here?
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我更多听到的是那些处在「边缘」的人——他们想尽办法要从积蓄里抠出每一分钱，好促成这次搬迁。部分原因在于，要拿到葡萄牙这里的 D7 签证，你得证明自己有达到一定水平的收入。而如果你能拿出一份来自这类产品的高收入证明，就更容易够到那个门槛。可问题就在于——正如我们在聊的——你解决了一个问题，却可能制造出另一个：因为你用的这个产品，其实并不符合你的长远利益。事情就变得复杂了。它能把你送到这儿来，可等你到了这儿，接下来又该怎么办？

turns.en: Yeah. Let me go back to you on this because there's obviously people who use something like JEPI for income, and it's also a little defensive.
turns.zh: 嗯。我想把话题拉回到你这边，因为显然有人会用像 JEPI 这样的产品来赚收入，而且它还带一点防御性。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Then there's people who use YieldMax, which is way more aggressive.
turns.zh: 也有人用 YieldMax，那就要激进得多了。

turns.en: Those two tickers. Kony, is it?
turns.zh: 这两个代码。是 Kony（CONY）吧？

turns.en: Kony.
turns.zh: Kony。

turns.en: C-O-N-Y, that's the YieldMax coin option income strategy, and JEPI, the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF.
turns.zh: C-O-N-Y，就是 YieldMax 的比特币期权收益策略（Coin Option Income Strategy）；还有 JEPI，也就是 JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF（摩根大通股票溢价收益 ETF）。

turns.en: That's J-E-P-I.
turns.zh: 这就是 J-E-P-I。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: If there's a spectrum, you know, one's on one end, the other's on the other, what does Kony yield? Like 150%, something crazy.
turns.zh: 如果说这中间有一条光谱，一个在这头、另一个在那头，那 Kony 的收益率有多少？得有 150% 吧，某种很夸张的数字。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，嗯。

turns.en: And Jeppe yields 8%. Yeah. I guess if you like getting income, if you were to say, just get total return, like buy the S & P 500 and then like sell a little bit, you have to pay capital gains taxes on that. So is there any advantage to gain the income or is it mostly psychological for these people where they just want to get the income mailed to them, sent to them, and even if they are taxed on it, it's not any worse than selling their total return and it's just easier than like monitoring their account. Is that generally what you find the advantages?
turns.zh: 而 JEPI 的收益率是 8%。对。我想，如果你就是喜欢拿现金流收入的话——假如你只是想拿总回报，比如直接买标普 500（S&P 500），然后需要时卖一点，那你是要为卖出部分缴纳资本利得税（capital gains taxes）的。那么拿收入到底有没有什么优势呢？还是说对这些人来讲主要是心理层面的——他们就是想收到寄来的、打过来的收入，哪怕这些收入也要交税，也并不比卖出总回报更吃亏，而且比盯着账户自己操作要省心得多？你观察下来，大家觉得优势大致就是这些吗？

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. When I was reporting, I kept thinking about people kept saying that they don't have to sell their investment to get income. To me, if it feels really psychological because the dividend income that you get from these derivative products are still taxed as ordinary income largely unlike the dividend stocks are taxed in a much lower bracket which is qualified dividends but for them like They also treat it as growth to a certain extent. For instance, if you put money into Kony or one of those YieldMax really high yielding products, you get maybe high double digit or triple digit yield. And they might have some leftover that month that they don't spend on their daily life. They put it back into that product. And to them, that's growth. Even though over time, the net asset value is eroding. So for them, yeah, it's the way that they're seeing yield is this, distribution is that, is very like a trigger point for them.
turns.zh: 嗯，嗯。我在做这篇报道的时候，好几个人反复提到的一点是：他们不用卖掉自己的投资就能拿到收入。对我来说，这真的更多是心理层面的，因为你从这些衍生品里拿到的分红收入，大部分仍然要按普通收入（ordinary income）来交税；不像分红股票（dividend stocks），那种是按低得多的税率征的，也就是合格分红（qualified dividends）。但对他们而言，这在某种程度上也被当成了「增长」。比如说，你把钱投进 Kony 或者 YieldMax 那种收益率高得吓人的产品，可能拿到高两位甚至三位数的收益率。他们那个月如果日常开销之外还有剩，就把剩下的钱再投回这个产品里。对他们来说，那就是增长——尽管随着时间推移，净值（net asset value）其实在被侵蚀。所以对他们而言，没错，他们看待「收益率」和「分红」的这种方式，是一个非常关键的触发点。

turns.en: Mark, say a client comes to you and says, hey, these things seem like they're great and here's my plan.
turns.zh: Mark，假设有位客户来找你，说：「嘿，这些东西看起来很棒，这是我的计划。」

turns.en: How would you talk to them about yield?
turns.zh: 你会怎么跟他们谈「收益率」这件事？

turns.en: Well, first off, I think that they're, you know, Kahneman, Tversky always said one of the things is, you know, losses loom larger than gains. And I think that's, one of the big things here is that I'm getting income in a good market and a bad market. Yes, it'll vary, but I don't, if I'm not looking at my, you know, my NAV honest, I'm getting this income. So, and as the old saying is, you know, you only take a loss when you sell it. Well, that's kind of, I think, part of the psychological point of this. But I do agree with the idea that don't treat, don't make your stock investments, your income investments. So I would, I'm more of the opinion that, you know, you treat, treat your bonds as your income and you can also supplement some of your, if you have gains in some of your stocks to supplement part of that. But I would, I don't want to force Force a stock to be my income, I guess is probably the easiest way to say that. I tell that to the clients we work with quite a bit is, you know, don't make it something it isn't.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，我想说的是，Kahneman 和 Tversky 一直讲的一句话是：损失比收益更让人揪心（losses loom larger than gains）。我觉得这里一个很关键的点就是：不管市场是好是坏，我都能拿到收入。是的，收入会有波动，但只要我不去看我的净值（NAV），我就是实实在在拿到了这笔收入。老话怎么说来着——「只有你卖出的时候，才算真正亏了」。我想这在某种程度上正是它的心理卖点所在。不过我也认同一个观点：别把你的股票投资当成你的收入来源。所以我更倾向于这么看：把你的债券当作收入来源，如果你手上有些股票有浮盈，也可以用它们来补充一部分收入。但我不想硬逼着一只股票去充当我的收入——这大概是最直白的说法了。我经常跟我们合作的客户讲这句话：别把一样东西变成它本来不是的样子。

turns.en: And that's because stock is effectively, you know, a share in something that's future profits, whereas fixed income is, hey, this is like what you're signed.
turns.zh: 这是因为，说到底，股票其实是你对未来利润的一份所有权份额；而固定收益产品则像是——嘿，这是你签约时约定好的东西……

turns.en: Up for, right? Like it's fixed for a reason. Yeah.
turns.zh: ……你签的就是这个数，对吧？就是说，它之所以叫「固定」，是有原因的。对。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Well, and the other part is too, is that, you know, even as a QQQI, it gives you 80% of the upside and it protects 75% of the downside, which is nice. It sounds soothing. Again, it goes back to, you know, the old Kahneman, you know, keeping, making sure you don't have losses. But the problem there is, is that bull markets and where actually the stock market historically, if you really want to look at rates of return, The real returns in the stock market are those abnormally high rate of return years. And when you cap those with these kind of type of investments, you're not going to get those real high stock market averages over time.
turns.zh: 嗯，还有一点也很重要：即便是像 QQQI 这样的产品，它能给你 80% 的上行空间、又能挡住 75% 的下行，这听起来很不错、也很让人安心。这又回到了 Kahneman 那套——确保你别亏钱。但问题在于，如果你真想看股市的回报率，牛市、以及历史上股市真正贡献回报的，恰恰是那些异常高的回报年份。而当你用这类投资把那些高回报给「封顶」（cap）之后，你就再也拿不到股市长期平均下来那种真正的高回报了。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Let me talk about that. I get that. That is somebody who's younger and has time. There's no way you'd want to do this. I mean, you should really just set it and forget it. Boo and chill. Wait 30 years. You'll beat all the active managers. Done deal. However, some people just have other life needs. If you get some of your return in the form of income, I was thinking about this and trying to work out if I would do it. The idea that you're getting money that you are spending on your life, it does take away the possibility that the market goes on like a huge crash. And at least you got yours for a little while. and were able to cash out and milk it like a cow and go surfing and write the next great American novel and hike in the Amazon. I mean, I suppose you could like store up all this money and then finally, what do you have a stack of money when you're like 80? I mean, there is some case to be, you know, carpe diem here. Thoughts on that?
turns.zh: 我来说说这一点，我理解。如果你还年轻、有的是时间，那你绝不该碰这种东西。你真应该「买了就放着别管」（set it and forget it）——买入然后躺平（boo and chill），等上 30 年，你就能跑赢所有主动型基金经理，板上钉钉。不过话说回来，有些人就是有别的现实需求。如果你的一部分回报是以收入的形式拿到的——我一直在琢磨这事儿，也在想要不要自己也这么干——你拿到的是花在自己生活上的钱，这确实就排除了那种「市场突然大崩盘」砸到你头上的可能性。至少你落袋为安了一阵子，能够套现，像挤牛奶一样把它挤出来，然后去冲浪、去写下一部伟大的美国小说、去亚马逊雨林徒步。我是说，反过来想，你也可以把钱一直攒着，可攒到最后呢？难道等到八十岁的时候，就为守着一大摞钱？所以这里多少还是有点「及时行乐」（carpe diem）的道理的。你怎么看？

turns.en: Well, I guess you'd say first off is that most of my clients, if not all of them are entrepreneurs. Even if you're 65, you plan out to 95, you still have a 30-year window that you're working towards. And that in and of itself is going to make a longer-term investing plan for people. The other part of this is living in Portugal, we have a 20% tax on capital gains and income. So with that being said, you could take. Something like this, and you're going to be taxed 20% on all of this every year, as opposed to if you had a stock and a bond portfolio, you could defer, or actually what happens if you hold for over nine years a stock in Portugal, a U.S. stock even, it's only going to be 19.6% tax rate as opposed to 28. So it's still, it plays in your favor to own stocks and own bonds in your portfolio and let them do their real job as opposed to just getting income because that's just going to, the taxes are going to really start eating into your living expenses.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想首先要说的是，我的客户里大多数——即便不是全部——都是创业者。哪怕你已经 65 岁，规划到 95 岁，你也还有一个为之努力的 30 年窗口。而这本身就会让人去做一个更长期的投资规划。另一方面，住在葡萄牙，我们对资本利得和收入都要征 20% 的税。这么说吧：你可以拿这样一笔产品，然后每年都要为它交 20% 的税；相比之下，如果你持有的是股票加债券的组合，你就可以递延纳税。实际上，在葡萄牙，如果你持有一只股票超过九年——哪怕是美国股票——税率只有 19.6%，而不是 28%。所以，在组合里持有股票和债券、让它们去干各自真正的活儿，对你其实更有利，而不是一味地去拿收入；因为光是税这一项，就会开始实实在在地蚕食你的生活开销。

turns.en: I do think Eric brings up a really good point that it's, there are compromises that these people are making. And in general, just It happens that people that I've talked to are all in their 40s and only one couple have kids, a three-year-old. But the other ones, they don't have kids. Some of them are single. Some of them have partners living this lifestyle with them. I always wonder, like, then what happens if you want to have a kid or you want to maybe send them to the really expensive schools or provide a better life for them? And also, actually, the Canadian couple that I talked to in the story, they're the most conservative ones, and they don't touch these high-yield ETFs. They have a bunch of other investments in the traditional conventional dividend stocks. And they traveled for 10 years and returned to Canada, had a child. They actually traveled, went back into the world with the kid for a bit longer, and they belong into this group that's called the World Schoolers. So there's a way to do this. And they told me that, like, It depends on your age period. Some people, maybe in their 30s and 40s, they want to do this lifestyle. They're not thinking too much about what will happen afterwards. But then you grow out of that and then you settle down. Maybe after you have a kid, you tend to trend towards this more stability in life. So it doesn't mean that people living this lifestyle are going to do this for life. It's just a way for them maybe to express themselves to explore the world at the moment.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得 Eric 提了一个特别好的点：这些人是在做各种妥协的。总的来说，碰巧我聊过的这些人都在四十多岁，其中只有一对有孩子——一个三岁的小孩；其他人都没有孩子，有的是单身，有的有伴侣一起过这种生活。我总是会想：那如果你之后想生孩子呢？或者想送他们去那种特别贵的学校、给他们提供更好的生活呢？还有，其实我在报道里聊到的那对加拿大夫妇，是最保守的一对，他们根本不碰这些高收益 ETF，而是持有一堆传统的、常规的分红股票。他们旅行了十年，然后回到加拿大、生了一个孩子。之后他们其实又带着孩子重新出发、在世界上多走了一段时间。他们属于一个叫做「世界学堂族」（World Schoolers）的群体。所以这条路是走得通的。他们跟我说，这要看你所处的人生阶段。有些人可能三四十岁的时候想过这种生活，并不会太多去想以后会怎样；但等你过了那个阶段、安定下来——也许是在有了孩子之后——你会更倾向于追求生活里的稳定。所以这并不意味着过这种生活的人会一辈子这么过下去。对他们来说，这也许只是在当下这个阶段，一种表达自我、探索世界的方式。

turns.en: And were your sources aware of the risks? I mean, obviously, they're probably aware of the compromises. But what about the risks of what could go wrong?
turns.zh: 那你的这些消息源，意识到风险了吗？我是说，他们显然大概清楚那些妥协。但那些「可能出岔子」的风险呢？

turns.en: Yeah. I've asked them, are you worried about a market crash? I asked every one of them, and they said they do. Because right now, there's just so much nervousness about the stock market crash. They said, I'll have to take on work if I... If I need to, I'll go back to the 40-hour work week. But actually, when I talked to Mark, Mark mentioned something really interesting. He's saying for people who have grit, they can make it work, even though on paper for financial advisors or for the regular eye, there's no way you can, but never underestimate grit.
turns.zh: 嗯。我问过他们：「你担心市场崩盘吗？」我每一个人都问了，他们都说担心。因为眼下大家对股市崩盘有太多紧张情绪了。他们说：「如果需要的话，我就去接活儿干；真有必要，我就回到每周 40 小时的工作制。」不过实际上，当我跟 Mark 聊的时候，Mark 提到了一件特别有意思的事。他说，对那些有韧劲（grit）的人来说，他们能让这条路走通——尽管在纸面上、在理财顾问或者普通人眼里，这根本不可能。但永远不要低估韧劲。

turns.en: And Mark, what did you mean by that? How does that grid express itself in what you see?
turns.zh: Mark，你这话是什么意思？在你看来，这种韧劲具体是怎么体现出来的？

turns.en: Well, first off, being an expat is hard. I mean, let's get around. There's a myriad of tax rules. There is a bureaucracy that you don't understand. My Portuguese don't even begin to tell you how bad I am at doing Portuguese. So you have all these built-in friction points that you're working with. So the people who only last a year or two here, that's not a bad experience for them. I think they learned something out of it, but a lot of times when they come back, it's because they just didn't have the, they didn't have a reason why they were coming and they thought it was a neat experience, but they didn't really understand that this was, there's a, you know, work to be done. You have to figure out the bureaucracy. and also how to figure out how to make your money work. And that in and of itself is a bitter, a bigger tell for me that they're going to make it or not. It's just, you know, are they, they have that grit, that ability to, you know, to put the shoes on every morning and make it work.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，当一个外籍侨居者（expat）是很难的。咱们打开天窗说亮话吧。这里有数不清的税务规则，有你根本搞不懂的官僚体系；我的葡萄牙语……就更别提我有多差了。所以你面对的是一堆天生的摩擦点。那些在这里只待了一两年就走的人，对他们来说这并不是一段糟糕的经历——我觉得他们从中学到了东西。但很多时候他们之所以又回来，是因为他们当初并没有一个「为什么要来」的理由，只是觉得这是一段挺新鲜的经历，却没真正意识到：这里头是有活儿要干的。你得去搞明白那套官僚体系，还得琢磨怎么让你的钱为你所用。而这一点本身，对我来说就是一个更大的信号，能看出他们到底能不能撑下去。说到底就是：他们有没有那股韧劲，那种每天早上把鞋穿上、然后把它跑通的能力。

turns.en: When I was in my twenties, I actually withdrew some of my 401k just to, um, party.
turns.zh: 我二十几岁的时候，还真从我的 401k 里取过一些钱出来，就为了……嗯，去狂欢。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: I was in Manhattan in the late nineties. And, uh, It was great. This was Clinton economy plus no cell phones. It was like a nice little window of time there. So now I'm older, got married, had kids.
turns.zh: 那会儿是九十年代末，我在曼哈顿。日子过得很爽。那是克林顿经济（Clinton economy），加上还没有手机，感觉就像是那么一段美好又难得的时光窗口。所以现在我年纪大了些，结了婚、有了孩子。

turns.en: How do you feel about that decision now?
turns.zh: 那你现在怎么看当年那个决定？

turns.en: You know what? I'm mixed. Compounding is so great. And the earlier you start, the better the compounding gets. However, you only live once.
turns.zh: 你知道吗？我的心情挺复杂的。复利（compounding）太美妙了，你开始得越早，复利的效果就越好。可是人这一辈子只活一次。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And I feel like I am not going to have a midlife crisis now because I did it all in my early, in my twenties. I went wild and I feel like that it just scratched. And in a way, maybe it was valuable. It's more of a mixed feeling. It's not like I'm dumb or I shouldn't have done that. So I think before you have kids, I remember my, my older, my older cousin who was like 10 years ahead of me in life all the time. She was washing dishes one day and she goes, he looked at me, he said, is there anything you want to do? Do it before you have kids. Cause after that it's over. And she was right. She was right. So it's kind of easy to save. You just become a working stiff, you're home every day and you let the money compound. But if you do have time on your hands, I mean, I don't know. I don't know.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得自己现在不会有中年危机了，因为我在二十几岁的时候就全都干过了。我疯玩了一场，感觉那种劲儿算是发泄掉了。某种程度上，那也许是有价值的。所以更多的是一种复杂的心情，并不是说我很蠢、或者当初就不该那么做。所以我觉得，在你有孩子之前——我记得我那位比我年长、人生大约领先我十岁的表姐，有一天她在洗碗，然后看着我跟我说：「有没有什么是你想去做的？趁还没生孩子赶紧去做，因为那之后就完了。」她说得对，她说得对。所以攒钱其实挺容易的：你就当个埋头苦干的打工人，每天按时回家，让钱去滚复利。但如果你手上有大把空闲时间，那……我是说，我也不知道，真说不好。

turns.en: It's complicated.
turns.zh: 这事儿挺复杂的。

turns.en: Um, so I get these people. I don't, I'm just not judgmental at all. And there are many ways to invest. And these products just do something that's convenient. They kind of just take this investment, give it to you in total return. And if you look at some of them in particular, like a Jepi, I believe the price performance is about flat or it's not that great, but you get the income. So it's not like you're like giving up your total return. You're flattish maybe. And you're just kind of cashing these checks, kind of like a bond, I guess. but it's 8% and not 3%, 4%. So I don't know. I can see both sides of this argument, but the evidence-based academic vanguard in me is like just voo and chill for 50 years. That's the best bet. But people are human and they have lives and needs. So it's not that black and white.
turns.zh: 嗯，所以我很能理解这些人。我一点都不评判他们，投资本来就有很多种方式。而这些产品做的，就是一件很方便的事：它们把这笔投资拿来，以总回报的形式交给你。如果你具体看其中一些产品，比如 JEPI，我记得它的价格表现基本是持平的、或者说不怎么样，但你能拿到收入。所以这并不是说你放弃了总回报，你也许就是打平，然后像收债券息票一样，一张一张地兑现这些「支票」——只不过收益是 8%，而不是 3%、4%。所以我说不好。这正反两面的道理我都看得到，但我内心那个讲证据、学院派、Vanguard 式的我在说：就买 VOO、然后躺平 50 年，这才是最好的选择。可人终究是人，有自己的生活和需求。所以这事儿没那么非黑即白。

turns.en: Mark, if Eric ends up on your sofa to tell you about his childhood.
turns.zh: Mark，如果哪天 Eric 跑到你家沙发上，跟你讲他小时候……

turns.en: In the 90s....
turns.zh: 九十年代的那些事……

turns.en: Or you could coach him. How would you... What wisdom would you offer him?
turns.zh: ……或者说你可以给他当教练。你会怎么……你会给他什么样的人生智慧？

turns.en: Actually, I can't... Yeah. I can't disagree with him. I tell people in Mexico.
turns.zh: 其实，我还真没法……对，我没法反驳他。我在墨西哥的时候也跟人说过这话。

turns.en: Come on, please.
turns.zh: 得了吧，拜托。

turns.en: Disagree with him.
turns.zh: 反驳他。

turns.en: It's like... A.
turns.zh: 这就像……啊。

turns.en: Joel Sarno right now that you agree with me. It's... I love it. Thank you.
turns.zh: Joel，你看，你现在都同意我了。这……我太喜欢了。谢谢。

turns.en: Well, yeah. Well, you know, you have to give me some of your Bloomberg food over there next time I visit. But....
turns.zh: 嗯，是啊。你知道，下次我过去的时候，你可得请我尝尝你们 Bloomberg 那边的美食。不过……

turns.en: No, but I really.
turns.zh: 不，不过我是真心……

turns.en: My colleagues that I work with laugh at me because I talk about clients all the time about this. I say, I'm just an optometrist dealing with money. And I go, does this look better? Does this look better? You know, covering my one eye or not. You tell me what your risk tolerance is, and I'll be happy to tell you what, you know, what those risks might entail. But in the end, you're going to call the shots. You know, what do you feel comfortable with? And sometimes it is spending your 401k money when you're 20 to have a good time. Do you blame somebody for that? No, because you learn something about yourself by doing it. I have people that I see all the time who are in their 60s. They retired and now they want to make this big move to Portugal. You know, complete life change. And they're trying to make this work. I'm not going to destroy their dream, but I'm also going to give them a dose of reality so that they understand potentially what the.
turns.zh: 我一起共事的同事都笑话我，因为我老跟客户念叨这个。我说：我简直就是个「配钱的验光师」——我会问「这样看更好吗？这样看更好吗？」你知道的，就像验光时遮住你一只眼那样。你告诉我你的风险承受能力，我很乐意告诉你这些风险可能意味着什么。但到头来，拍板的人是你。你觉得怎样才安心？有时候，安心的选择就是二十岁的时候把你的 401k 花掉、去好好玩一场。你会因此责怪一个人吗？不会，因为通过这么做，你更了解自己了。我常常见到一些人，都六十多岁了，退了休，现在想大老远搬到葡萄牙来——彻底的人生转变。他们在努力让这件事成。我不会去击碎他们的梦想，但我也一定会给他们一剂现实的清醒药，让他们明白这里头潜在的……

turns.en: Risks risks are yeah the um when we were writing the story i wanted really to highlight the the positive and negative side of this and and the risks involved um but the feedback that i got after the story came out was my friends asking me oh maybe i should recalculate my investment how do i do this yeah how do i retire at 45 um But I think it's also like the FIRE movement and the digital nomad movement is even gaining more traction nowadays because AI, because of AI. I'm seeing like posts or forums, people discussing like, okay, if there's a future where AI potentially could replace our jobs or threaten our future earning potential, maybe I should front load all of that now. I should like earn as much money as I can to FIRE to retire early so that I don't have to deal with that kind.
turns.zh: ……风险，风险是什么。对。嗯，我们写这篇报道的时候，我是真的很想把它积极的一面、消极的一面，还有其中涉及的风险，都好好呈现出来。但报道发出来之后，我收到的反馈是——我朋友们跑来问我：「哎，也许我该重新算算我的投资了，这要怎么弄？对，我要怎么才能在 45 岁退休？」嗯。不过我觉得，这也跟 FIRE（财务独立、提前退休）运动和数字游民（digital nomad）运动如今越来越火有关，而且某种程度上是因为 AI。我看到不少帖子和论坛里，大家在讨论：如果未来 AI 有可能取代我们的工作、威胁到我们将来的赚钱能力，那也许我应该现在就把这一切「提前堆满」（front load）。我应该趁现在尽可能多赚钱，好 FIRE、好提前退休，这样就不必去面对那种局面了。

turns.en: Of This is the world that Eric was ready for when he was, you know, years younger.
turns.zh: ……的局面。这就是当年 Eric 还年轻好几岁的时候，早早为之做好准备的那个世界。

turns.en: I will say now that I'm older, though, the whole fire thing, like the idea of just like retiring at 40, I could do it. I would set a schedule for myself, but I would have to half work. I think they overrate sitting there with nothing to do. But sounds like if they're going like I would wake up and I would go for a long jog and then I would do work for a couple hours, have lunch, take a nap. do work for like two hours and then I would do like fun stuff and, you know, go swimming in the ocean.
turns.zh: 不过我得说，现在我年纪大了些，对整个 FIRE 那套——就是四十岁直接退休的想法——我其实做得到。我会给自己排一张日程表，但我恐怕得半工作半退休。我觉得他们高估了「啥也不干、干坐着」这件事。不过听他们的描述，如果按他们那种来法，我大概会这么过：早上起来先去长跑一大圈，然后干两个小时的活儿，吃个午饭，睡个午觉，再干两个小时的活儿，然后就去做些好玩的事，比如去海里游泳。

turns.en: That's what Mark's doing in Portugal. Yeah, I know.
turns.zh: 这不就是 Mark 在葡萄牙过的日子嘛。是啊，我知道。

turns.en: Is that your schedule, Mark? But I would want to have like five hours of work in there, I think.
turns.zh: 这是你的日程吗，Mark？不过我想，我大概会希望里头排上五个小时的工作。

turns.en: But yeah.
turns.zh: 不过，是啊。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So I think you also, it might be overrated, this idea of this, I don't know, this fire thing. Like you could have fun while you're saving. That's why I kind of like the situation, the nomads thing. They are investing while at the same time having fun and not waiting for this final day where it's all over and it's like office space. I did nothing and it was absolutely everything I thought it could be. I think that life is a little overrated. You see some of these really rich guys retire and they go back to work because they probably drive their partners crazy and they probably go a little loony.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，这个……我也说不好，这个 FIRE 的想法，可能也被高估了。就是说，你完全可以在攒钱的同时过得开心。这也是为什么我挺喜欢「数字游民」这种活法的：他们一边投资，一边享受生活，而不是死等着那个「一切都结束」的最后一天——就像《上班一条虫》（Office Space）里那样，「我什么都没干，可那就是我想象中圆满的一切」。我觉得那种生活有点被高估了。你会看到有些特别有钱的人退休之后又回去工作了，大概是因为他们把另一半逼疯了，也可能是他们自己有点闲出毛病、要犯浑了。

turns.en: We've been talking a lot about the 40-somethings and how they're able to use this. I guess the other side is actually people who are retired or.
turns.zh: 我们已经聊了很多四十多岁的人、以及他们怎么用上这些产品。我想另一头，其实是那些已经退休、或者……

turns.en: or on the brink of retirement.
turns.zh: ……或者正处在退休边缘的人。

turns.en: And how does that dynamic with these products change that calculus a little bit?
turns.zh: 那么配上这些产品之后，这种情况会怎么稍微改变一下那笔账（calculus）？

turns.en: I'd say that, you know, if you're trying to stretch every cent out because you need it, because this, let's put it this way. Let's say that your dream always has been to live in Europe. You always wanted to do it. That was your dream for retirement. And life didn't deal you all the cards you wanted to, you know, to make it work easily. But you can make it work with one of these products. Okay. And you could make the, you know, make the D7 visa as we have it here, which that is primarily retirement visa for a lot of people moving to Portugal. So you can make the numbers work. Am I to say no to somebody's, you know, lifelong dream?
turns.zh: 我会这么说：如果你是在想尽办法抠出每一分钱，因为你确实需要——这么讲吧，假设你的梦想一直是住在欧洲，你一直都想这么做，那是你退休时的梦想，可生活并没有把你想要的那几张牌都发给你、让你轻轻松松就能实现。但靠这类产品里的某一个，你能让它成。好，你就能凑够数字，拿到我们这里的 D7 签证——对很多搬来葡萄牙的人来说，那主要就是一种退休签证。所以你能把这笔账算得过来。那我难道要去对一个人一辈子的梦想说「不」吗？

turns.en: No. No.
turns.zh: 不，不。

turns.en: Not at all.
turns.zh: 当然不会。

turns.en: But I would certainly want to have them enter it with their eyes open to understand, you know, this is a risk. This is a risk that are entailed. And if you still want to do it, more power to you. I mean, it's your life to live.
turns.zh: 但我一定希望他们在开始的时候是睁大眼睛的，明白这是一份风险、明白这里头附带的种种风险。而如果你了解之后仍然想去做，那就尽管放手去做——毕竟这是你自己的生活，得由你自己来过。

turns.en: Joel, one of the sayings we have on our team.
turns.zh: Joel，我们团队里有一句常挂在嘴边的话。

turns.en: The Bloomberg Intelligence PCF crew.
turns.zh: 就是 Bloomberg Intelligence 的那个 ETF 团队。

turns.en: Want to retire in Europe? Invest in the U.S. The U.S. stock market is a big part of it. And if you use JEPI or VU, I just think you're still at least in the right spot. And honestly, let's be honest, some of this is like a bull market function. I don't know if you could do all this in a bear market.
turns.zh: 「想在欧洲退休？那就投资美国。」美国股市是其中很大的一块。如果你用的是 JEPI 或者 VOO，我至少觉得你还是站在对的位置上的。而且老实说，咱们实话实说，这里头有一部分其实是牛市的产物。我不确定在一轮熊市里，你还能不能把这一切都玩转。

turns.en: Well, what would happen with these products in a bear market or a significant downturn?
turns.zh: 那么，在一轮熊市或者一次大幅回撤里，这些产品会怎么样？

turns.en: There's two parts to this. One is that a significant bear market, you're probably going to do okay in month one, two, three, four, and five. My concern is beyond that. Because At those points now, the potential for you to start dipping into your principal, your NAV on this is going to get greater and greater. The chances are going to happen. That's where I'm really concerned. I mean, like in last year where we had the 20% correction with the tariffs, that one barely showed up because you're you're writing calls on a month-to-month basis on most of these products. So it's like every month, you know, you're re-evaluating for a new test at school, you know? So that part, I think, is if you had a long, prolonged, I mean, a very prolonged bear market, that's when I would be concerned.
turns.zh: 这里有两个层面。第一，在一轮严重的熊市里，第一、二、三、四、五个月你多半都还扛得住。我担心的是再往后。因为到了那个时候，你开始蚕食自己本金（principal）、蚕食净值（NAV）的可能性就会越来越大，而且这种事儿真的会发生——这才是我真正担心的地方。我是说，就像去年关税（tariffs）引发的那次 20% 的回撤，它几乎没怎么显现出来，因为这类产品大多是在按月卖出看涨期权（write calls）。所以就好像每个月你都在为学校里的一场新考试重新评估一次，你懂吧？所以从这个角度看，如果是那种旷日持久、非常漫长的熊市，那才是我会担心的时候。

turns.en: And that long, prolonged bear market is the key here because actually I talked to some financial advisors and investors and There's a sense that we're very unlikely to have a long, prolonged bear market because so many Americans' wealth are tied up in the stock market. And you almost see like a taco trade that we've been talking a long time. So people think that the government won't allow the stock market to have a prolonged downturn. Hold on.
turns.zh: 而那种旷日持久的熊市，正是这里的关键。因为其实我采访过一些理财顾问和投资者，有一种共识是：我们很不太可能遇到一轮漫长的熊市，因为太多美国人的财富都绑在股市里了。你几乎能看到一种我们一直在聊的「TACO 交易」（taco trade）。所以人们觉得，政府不会允许股市经历一场旷日持久的下跌。等等——

turns.en: Who are these people?
turns.zh: 这些人都是谁啊？

turns.en: Because I literally have been saying that all year. I wrote a note.
turns.zh: 因为这事儿我整整一年都在讲。我写过一份研究报告（note）。

turns.en: And Eric.
turns.zh: 还有 Eric。

turns.en: The stock market, it's too important to fail. It's the electric grid of the retirement. And I think it's basically people are depending on it to replace social security. And so I agree. Now, 10%, I think they'll let it go down. But like 2030, I just don't know if we'll have a crash ever again.
turns.zh: 股市太重要，输不起（too important to fail）。它就像是退休体系的电网。我觉得，从根本上说，人们正指望着它来取代社保（social security）。所以我同意这个判断。不过 10% 的跌幅，我想他们会放任它跌下去；但要说到 20%、30%，我就真不确定我们将来还会不会再遇到一次崩盘了。

turns.en: Well- If I could just jump in, Bram Kaplan of JP Morgan last year, he wrote a piece that said, a key force of the recent suppression of the market volatility is because of these ETFs that we're seeing. So that is an interesting part too, is that maybe all of these types of ETFs that we're talking about right now are actually suppressing the volatility in and of themselves.
turns.zh: 那个——请容我插一句。JP Morgan 的 Bram Kaplan 去年写过一篇文章，说近期市场波动率被压制住的一个关键力量，正是因为我们看到的这些 ETF。所以这也是很有意思的一点：也许我们正在聊的这一整类 ETF，本身就在压制着波动率。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So I've thought about this. I honestly think Vanguard in particular- help solve investor behavior because they have these products that you can marry. And so people just are like buying their vu, doesn't matter what happens. You're not going to shake them out. And they do suppress volatility to a degree. But I think that's probably good.
turns.zh: 这事儿我也想过。说实话，我尤其觉得 Vanguard 帮了大忙，因为它有这些你可以「长相厮守」的产品，从而帮助改善了投资者的行为。所以人们就是不停地买他们的 VOO，管它发生什么都不动摇，你没法把他们吓跑。而且它们在一定程度上的确压制了波动率。但我觉得这大概是件好事。

turns.en: Because they just show up, right? Again, it goes down, they double down.
turns.zh: 因为他们就是会一直出现，对吧？市场再跌，他们就加倍买入（double down）。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: They're not like, oh, my five-star manager is now underperforming and they leave, which is probably the worst time to leave. Then they go buy the next five-star manager, which is the worst time to buy that. People were very poorly behaved for many decades. I think Vanguard helped solve behavior. So I think it's a win. Some people complain about that. I'm like, I get it. Isn't that good?
turns.zh: 他们不会说「哦，我那位五星基金经理现在跑输大盘了」，然后就走人——而那往往是最糟糕的离场时机；接着他们又去买下一位五星基金经理，而那又是最糟糕的买入时机。很多年里，人们的行为都很糟糕。我觉得 Vanguard 帮忙改善了行为。所以我认为这是一件好事。有些人对此有怨言，我就想：我懂，可这难道不好吗？

turns.en: I mean, sure.
turns.zh: 我是说，那当然。

turns.en: I do think we call it the Vanguard put. If the market is going down, there is a buffer there because the Vanguard bid is always there. It doesn't mean the market won't go down, but it probably helps it from going down more.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，我们管它叫「Vanguard 看跌期权」（the Vanguard put）。如果市场在往下走，那里就有一层缓冲，因为 Vanguard 的买盘始终都在。这并不意味着市场不会跌，但它大概能帮着别让它跌得太狠。

turns.en: Mark, as we wrap up here, I'm curious, as a financial advisor, how much do ETFs factor into your day job and how you're talking to clients?
turns.zh: Mark，我们快到尾声了，我很好奇：作为一名理财顾问，ETF 在你日常工作、以及你跟客户沟通中，占多大比重？

turns.en: They are definitely a piece of it. We tend to be more on the actual buying of individual bonds, laddering out for the fixed income side. Just an easier process. Clients understand the risk and the holding of them that way. We do a lot of direct indexing because of the taxes here in Portugal. It works better, gives you a better return, generally speaking. But when we get into a lot of these international, like for instance, last year, the European markets did extremely well. A good portion of that was purely currency. So that worked out well. So I guess you'd say we use ETFs wherever they make sense. And it's also in an account, a smaller account, that's very efficient for them. And it's harder to do a direct indexing with a smaller client.
turns.zh: 它们肯定是其中一块。在固定收益这边，我们往往更倾向于直接买入个别的债券、做成阶梯式（laddering），流程更简单，客户也更容易理解这样持有它们的风险。我们也做很多直接指数化投资（direct indexing），因为在葡萄牙这里的税务关系，它效果更好、通常能给你更好的回报。但当我们涉及很多国际的部分时——比如说去年，欧洲市场表现得极其出色，其中很大一部分纯粹是汇率带来的，所以那回效果很好。所以我想说，只要 ETF 说得通，我们就会用。而且在一个较小的账户里，ETF 的效率非常高；相比之下，给一个较小的客户做直接指数化投资就要难得多。

turns.en: I should have asked this earlier. Are most of your clients American expats? Or are you working with Americans?
turns.zh: 这个我本该早点问的：你的客户大多数都是旅居海外的美国人（American expats）吗？还是说你服务的是身在美国的美国人？

turns.en: 100%. 100% working with expats?
turns.zh: 100%？100% 都是旅居海外的客户？

turns.en: Just Americans. They're either thinking about it or they're actually over here.
turns.zh: 就是美国人。他们要么是在盘算着要过来，要么就是人已经在这边了。

turns.en: Mark Zichia, thanks for joining us on Trillions.
turns.zh: Mark、Zitia，感谢二位做客 Trillions。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Bye.
turns.zh: 再见。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。
